article.nlp.title: Toxic Comment Classification
article.nlp.subtitle: This project focuses on automatic toxicity detection in online comments using a classic NLP pipeline and a lightweight neural network.
article.nlp.overview.title: Project overview
article.nlp.overview.text: Online platforms generate massive amounts of user text, sometimes containing insults, threats, or hateful speech. The goal here is to detect six toxicity categories (toxic, severe toxic, obscene, threat, insult, identity hate) along with an additional not toxic label (corresponding to comments that do not contain any of the six other categories). The model is multi-label, meaning that a single comment can activate several labels at the same time.
article.nlp.dataset.title: Dataset
article.nlp.dataset.text: The model is based on the Toxic Comment Classification dataset from Kaggle. It contains around 159,000 comments, each annotated with six binary labels. The classes are highly imbalanced: threat, severe toxic, and identity hate are rare, while most comments are non-toxic. This imbalance makes learning and generalization more difficult for minority classes.
article.nlp.methodology.title: General methodology
article.nlp.methodology.text: The pipeline follows a straightforward structure: text preprocessing with spaCy, extraction of 300-dimensional embedding vectors, aggregation of word vectors into a sentence representation, then classification through a multilayer perceptron. The goal is not to reach state-of-the-art performance, but to build a compact, interpretable, and easy-to-explain architecture.
article.nlp.preprocessing.title: Text preprocessing
article.nlp.preprocessing.text: Preprocessing is done with spaCy (en_core_web_md). The steps include tokenization, stopword removal, lemmatization, filtering non-alphabetic tokens, projecting each lemma into a 300-dimensional embedding vector, then aggregating vectors through simple summation. This representation loses word order information, but still captures enough semantic signal to train a coherent model.
article.nlp.embeddings.title: Feature extraction (embeddings)
article.nlp.embeddings.text: spaCy’s pretrained embeddings provide a 300-dimensional vector for each known word. Semantically similar words tend to occupy nearby regions in vector space. A comment representation is obtained by summing the vectors of its words, which avoids training a full language model and allows very fast inference times.
article.nlp.architecture.title: Neural network architecture
article.nlp.architecture.text: The classifier is a multilayer perceptron (MLP) with a 300-dimensional input layer, three hidden layers of size 100 using tanh activations, and a 7-dimensional output layer (one output per label). The optimizer used is Adam with a constant learning rate. The architecture remains simple, but sufficient to model the main patterns of the dataset.
article.nlp.training.title: Training and evaluation
article.nlp.training.text: The dataset is split into 80% training and 20% testing. Because the task is multi-label, evaluation relies on precision, recall, and F1-score, both globally and per class. The Adam optimizer automatically adjusts the learning rate of each weight and provides stable convergence for this type of problem.
article.nlp.results.title: Results
article.nlp.results.text: The model achieves solid performance on frequent classes such as toxic and insult, while rarer categories (threat, identity hate, severe toxic) remain harder to predict reliably. Despite its simplicity, the multi-label classifier produces coherent scores on the majority of comments, making it a good compromise between readability and performance.
article.nlp.example.title: Prediction example
article.nlp.example.text: For the comment “You're a disgusting idiot.”, the model will typically activate the Toxic, Insult, and Obscene labels, but not Threat or Identity Hate, and it will not classify the comment as Not Toxic. This type of example illustrates the model’s ability to detect multiple facets of toxicity within the same sentence.
article.nlp.limitations.title: Model limitations
article.nlp.limitations.text: Several important limitations remain: summing embeddings removes word order and grammatical structure, rare classes still produce low F1-scores, and the MLP cannot capture long-range dependencies or contextual nuance. In addition, the pretrained embeddings are not specialized for toxicity detection and are not fine-tuned during training.
article.nlp.future.title: Possible improvements
article.nlp.future.text: Possible improvements include replacing embedding summation with transformer-based models (BERT, RoBERTa), introducing attention mechanisms to better exploit context, artificially augmenting data for rare classes, or testing optimization variants such as AdamW.

article.nlp.note.title: Personal note
article.nlp.note.text: This project allowed me to deepen my understanding of classic NLP pipelines, pretrained embeddings, multi-label classification, and neural network optimization. It also shows that a simple architecture can be surprisingly effective when combined with solid preprocessing.
